newsitem.title: USA: Rubin warns against revoking China trade ties.
newsitem.headline: Rubin warns against revoking China trade ties.

text.p: Revoking favored trade status for China would undermine U.S. economic and security interests and might harm efforts to promote stability in Hong Kong after July 1, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned on Thursday.

In a speech to the U.S.-China Business Council, Rubin weighed in heavily against congressional efforts to deny China "most favored nation" trading status and to link the issue to the handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1.

"Severing trade ties with China will not isolate China. It will isolate the United States," Rubin said, reducing U.S. ability to participate in the most dynamic economic region in the world at a time when Asian economies are integrating.

"Revoking normal trade relations with China would also harm Hong Kong in the name of supporting it," Rubin said. He noted that a coalition of Hong Kong human rights leaders, the current government in Hong Kong and others have warned that cutting trade ties with China would be "exactly the wrong step if our objective is to preserve an autonomous and free Hong Kong."

Earlier this week, Senate Foreign relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms introduced a resolution to deny China its MFN status in trade with the United States. A growing trade deficit with China as well as concern about Hong Kong's future under Chinese rule after Britain hands over the colony on July 1 has helped fuel U.S. lawmakers' sentiment against China.
Rubin said the rising trade deficit partly reflected the fact that companies from other Asian countries were shifting their production to China.
He said the Clinton administration was keenly interested in seeing Hong Kong remain a key Asian financial center.
"This administration has made it clear that erosion of democracy and human rights in Hong Kong after the transition would be of grave concern to us," Rubin said.

The Treasury chief acknowledged that it was "tougher than ever" to resist calls from Capitol Hill to act against normal trade relations with China and that "a broader range of the political spectrum" now wanted action.
But he called upon U.S. business interests to back the Clinton administration's efforts to block Congress from revoking MFN status for China.
"I urge you to let your voice be heard," Rubin said.

The Treasury Secretary posed the issue of stable trade ties as one of promoting not only U.S. economic interests but also as a way of influencing the Asian trade giant on other matters like greater political freedoms for its citizens.

Rubin said normal trade ties with China were "a prerequisite for ensuring stability in Hong Kong, making progress on helping to establish a more open economy in China, integrating China into the global economy and dealing with human rights issues in China."
